confidence_why: No description of Gowro stress exists: Baart 2003 only guesses, with a question mark, that Gowro is a Shina-type language (lexically placed stress on a mora that carries a high tone), and the Hallberg 1992 survey wordlist marks stress on varying syllables while stating that its transcriptions have had no phonological analysis.

catalog_quote: The phonological analysis of the three other languages and dialects (Š, G and B) has been conducted less thoroughly, although a final analysis would generally show only minor differences. ... The lemmata from B and G have not been analyzed in this way. This means the following: in the majority of cases, accent marking of the G words only indicates the place of the accent. It does not indicate whether the accent is rising or falling. ... since B and G appear to have similar cases of accent shift under specific conditions ..., it is to be expected that the accent systems of B and G are quite similar to those of J. ... Indus Kohistani has two pitch accents, one rising and the other falling.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated for Gowro anywhere. Baart only suspects (with a question mark) that Gowro is tonal and tentatively groups it with the 'Shina-type' systems (lexically placed stress on one mora carrying a high tone), by analogy with its neighbours Indus Kohistani and Shina. The only first-hand data are the stress-marked field transcriptions in Hallberg's 1992 survey wordlist (column GAB), where the mark falls on different syllables in different words (initial 'nothu0, 'bVli; final su'rVt, hàlà'li), i.e. lexically variable placement, but the survey explicitly disclaims phonological analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author explicitly flags Gowro's tonal status as uncertain (question mark) and the classification as tentative.
new_statements.domain_note: Survey-level typological table with no Gowro data; 'Shina-type' is Baart's label for languages where stress is lexically assigned to one mora and realised as a high tone on that mora (Indus Kohistani, Shina, Burushaski, Palula are the certain members). Nothing is said about word vs phrase domain or citation forms for Gowro.
new_statements.identity_note: Gowro = Gabaro = the Gabar Khel clan language of Mahrin village (Kolai area, east bank of the Indus, District Kohistan), glottocode gowr1239, ISO gwf; Hallberg 1992 warns it must not be confused with Gawri (= Kalami/Gawri, gawr1245) of Swat. Zoller's 2005 Indus Kohistani dictionary treats 'Gabār' as a local variety of Indus Kohistani (indu1241) and Bashir equates it with Gowro; Hallberg's 61-63% lexical similarity between Gowro and Indus Kohistani and Jettmar's informants' denial of separateness show the language/dialect status is unsettled. Baart 2003 and Hallberg 1992 both refer to the Mahrin Gabar Khel variety.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has Gowro as 'undetermined' and the only prior statement is Baart 2003's hedged 'Yes?' tone / 'Shina-type' guess. Zoller 2005, from his own fieldwork on Gabār (consultant Muhammad Zaman), supplies primary data: Gabār words carry a lexical accent whose place is marked per lemma, and the system is expected to be a two-way (rising/falling) pitch accent system like Jijālī Indus Kohistani and Shina. This is compatible with and firms up Baart's 'Shina-type' tonal-accent classification; it does not give a positional stress rule, so it moves the record from 'undetermined' toward 'pitch accent, lexical placement', with the rising/falling contrast for Gabār itself flagged by the author as unv…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Zoller treats Gabār (= Gowro) as a lexical pitch accent language of the Indus Kohistani/Shina type: every Gabār lemma in the dictionary carries an accent mark on one syllable, and the place of that accent is a per-word lexical fact (dictionary G entries show it on initial, medial and final syllables, e.g. údi 'wooden post', kut.úlu 'filled', katákh 'name of a month', utéy 'glacier', agár 'first'). For Jijālī Indus Kohistani he establishes two contrastive pitch accents (rising vs falling, 'many minimal pairs', one accent per morpheme, p. 24, p. 26 rule 2) and he expects the Gabār system to be 'quite similar', citing parallel accent-shift behaviour; but for Gabār the rising/falling value was never checked instrumentally, so the G accent marks record accent PLACE only. No statement of a fixed or weight-predictable default position is given for Gabār (or for J).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Gabār. For J compounds he marks a dominant 'nucleus' accent vs weaker accents ((n1)/(n2) notation, p. 28 rule 12); layer-II suffixes/postpositions lose their accent entirely (rule 11).
new_statements.exceptions: For J (expected to carry over to G): rising accent on the ultima shifts rightward onto a layer-I declensional suffix, falling accent is static (rule 6, pp. 26-27); rising/falling contrast neutralized on short vowels in polysyllables and in monosyllables not closed by n, m, r, l, ṛ (rules 3-5); CV words always falling; accent values change in compounding, reduplication, derivation and verbal mood (rule 10). Author's explicit caveat: G accent analysis 'conducted less thoroughly', not tonologized with the speech analyzer.
new_statements.identity_note: Zoller's 'Gabār (G) (also called Gowro)' is the language of gowr1239, spoken opposite Jijāl on the east bank of the Indus (village Maharīn named as a Gabār-speaking village, p. 7); he treats it as a separate small Dardic language adjacent to, and heavily influenced by, Indus Kohistani and Kohistani Shina, not as a dialect of Indus Kohistani. The fully analysed pitch accent rules (ch. 2 sec. 3) are stated for the Jijālī (J) variety of Indus Kohistani (indu1241) and are only projected onto Gabār by the author; the Gabār-specific evidence is the accent-place marking on the roughly 260 G-tagged lemmata plus his remark on parallel accent-shift behaviour.
